questions.stem: Which gas do plants excrete in daylight?

options.text: Oxygen, because photosynthesis produces more than respiration uses
options.explanation: Surplus oxygen from faster photosynthesis is the daylight waste.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, because photosynthesis makes it
options.explanation: Photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide; it releases oxygen.
Nitrogen plays no part in plant metabolism here.
Transpiration happens, but the excretion asked about is the gas pair.

questions.stem: What do plants do with carbon dioxide at night?

options.explanation: Conversion needs photosynthesis, which has stopped.

options.text: They produce it by respiration and it diffuses out
options.explanation: Respiration runs without light, so carbon dioxide becomes the surplus gas.

options.text: They absorb extra carbon dioxide for storage
options.explanation: Nothing stores it; in darkness the plant makes more than it can use.

options.text: They stop producing any waste at all
options.explanation: Respiration never stops, so waste keeps coming.

questions.stem: Why is gas excretion in plants a passive process?

options.explanation: Thinness speeds diffusion but does not make it passive.
Photosynthesis creates the gradient; the diffusion itself is unpowered.

options.text: The gases simply diffuse down their concentration gradients
options.explanation: No pump or transport protein is needed; the gradient does the work.

options.text: Because the stomata are always wide open
options.explanation: Stomata open and close; openness is not the passivity.

questions.stem: During a bright day, what is the net effect on the two gases?

options.text: More carbon dioxide produced than used
options.explanation: That is the night-time balance.
Exact balance happens at a particular low light intensity, not in bright light.
Both keep moving; only the net balance shifts.

options.text: More oxygen produced than used, and less carbon dioxide released than used
options.explanation: Photosynthesis dominates, so oxygen accumulates and carbon dioxide is drawn down.

questions.stem: Through which structures do the waste gases leave the leaf?

options.explanation: The stomata are the pores the gases drift through.
Roots take up water and ions; they are not this exit.
The cuticle is a barrier, not a pore.
Xylem carries water upwards inside the plant.

questions.stem: Name the two waste gases of plant metabolism.
State when each gas becomes surplus in a plant.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen is surplus in the light when photosynthesis outruns respiration; carbon dioxide is surplus in the dark when only respiration runs.

questions.stem: Explain why the same gas can be a raw material by day and a waste by night.
questions.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide and releases oxygen while light lasts, but in darkness only respiration runs, consuming oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide; the direction of the faster process decides which gas is in surplus, so each gas swaps roles as the light changes.

questions.stem: A greenhouse keeper keeps lights on all night. Predict the gas exchange and explain why.
questions.modelAnswer: With light supplied, photosynthesis continues through the night, so the plant keeps consuming carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen; the usual night-time pattern of net carbon dioxide release is replaced by a daytime-style exchange in which oxygen is the surplus gas.
